target.title: Neural speech recognition: continuous phoneme decoding using spatiotemporal representations of human cortical activity
target.version: Accepted Manuscript (JNE-101252.R1) of the article published as J. Neural Eng. 13 (2016) 056004

read.pdf: No PDF supplied; read text-extracted captions for Figs. 1–9 and Tables 1–5.

target.first_public_basis: Crossref published-online 2016-08-03 (date_epub assertion; received 2016-03-18, accepted 2016-06-21); print issue 2016-10. Wiki source text is the IOP Accepted Manuscript of the same article (manifest says version_of_record: manifest error).

entries.text: Novelty claim: to the authors' knowledge, prior published work had not described benefits of ASR techniques for perceived continuous neural speech decoding in a single-speaker setting.
entries.condition: Authors' literature-scope claim; continuous perceived speech, single-speaker environment.
entries.quote: to the best of our knowledge, no published work has described the potential beneﬁts of using ASR techniques to decode perceived continuous speech from neural signals in a single-speaker environment.

entries.text: The authors frame the work as an initial, proof-of-concept NSR system intended to inform future research, not as a finished speech prosthesis.
entries.condition: Offline phoneme decoding from perceived English speech using ECoG.

entries.text: Sensing is subdural ECoG local field potentials; the input representation is high-gamma power from STG and neighboring cortex, arranged as spatiotemporal high-gamma windows (HGWs).
entries.condition: Perceived English speech; implanted cortical arrays; features span selected electrodes and multiple time points.
entries.quote: performs continuous phoneme recognition on English stimuli with arbitrary vocabulary sizes using the high gamma band power of local ﬁeld potentials in the STG

entries.text: The system combines an LDA phoneme-likelihood model, a phonemic n-gram language model, and HMM/Viterbi decoding to produce a maximum-a-posteriori phoneme sequence.
entries.condition: 38 Arpabet phonemes plus /sp/; basic additive-smoothed 4-gram LM; offline decoding.
entries.quote: The system implements a Viterbi decoder that incorporates phoneme likelihood estimates from a linear discriminant analysis model and transition probabilities from an n-gram phonemic language model.

entries.text: The cohort comprised three volunteer epilepsy patients undergoing treatment at UCSF; all had left-hemisphere language dominance, while subject C had right-hemisphere ECoG coverage.
entries.condition: Human clinical cohort; subjects A–C; ECoG arrays implanted for seizure-focus localization.

entries.text: Each implanted array had 256 electrodes with 1.17 mm exposed contacts and 4 mm center-to-center spacing; ECoG was sampled at approximately 3052 Hz.
entries.unit: electrodes; mm contact diameter; mm spacing; Hz sampling rate
entries.condition: Per subject; arrays covered cortex including STG; subjects A/B left hemisphere, C right hemisphere.

entries.text: TIMIT comprised 499 phonetically transcribed stimuli, approximately 25 minutes total, from 402 speakers (286 male speakers produced 354 stimuli; 116 female speakers produced 145).
entries.unit: stimuli; minutes; speakers; male speakers; male stimuli; female speakers; female stimuli
entries.condition: TIMIT; used for feature and decoder parameter optimization; subject C did not hear the full stimulus set.

entries.text: The Gump set comprised 382 reenacted Forrest Gump samples: 91 words, 175 phrases, and 116 dialog samples, produced in equal numbers by one male and one female speaker; total duration was about 43 minutes, about 24 minutes excluding silence.
entries.unit: stimuli; word stimuli; phrase stimuli; dialog stimuli; stimuli per speaker; minutes total; non-silence minutes
entries.condition: Two fixed speakers; each stimulus was presented at least once per subject; phonetic labels obtained by forced alignment followed by manual segmentation.
entries.quote: It contained 91 single word (0.3–1 s duration), 175 phrase (0.4–2.4 s duration), and 116 dialog (4.5–19.9 s duration) speech samples, with each speaker producing 191 of the samples.

entries.text: TIMIT data for subject A: 29 minutes non-silence, 54 minutes total, 1092 presentations, mean 2.19 presentations per unique stimulus.
entries.unit: minutes non-silence; minutes total; presentations; presentations per stimulus
entries.condition: Subject A, TIMIT stimulus presentations; the full TIMIT set had 499 unique stimuli.

entries.text: TIMIT data for subject B: 31 minutes non-silence, 59 minutes total, 1197 presentations, mean 2.40 presentations per unique stimulus.
entries.unit: minutes non-silence; minutes total; presentations; presentations per stimulus
entries.condition: Subject B, TIMIT stimulus presentations; the full TIMIT set had 499 unique stimuli.

entries.text: TIMIT data for subject C: 11 minutes non-silence, 21 minutes total, 412 presentations, mean 0.83 presentations per unique stimulus.
entries.unit: minutes non-silence; minutes total; presentations; presentations per stimulus
entries.condition: Subject C, TIMIT stimulus presentations; subject C did not receive the complete TIMIT stimulus set.

entries.text: Gump data for subject A: 47 minutes non-silence, 87 minutes total, 847 presentations, mean 2.22 presentations per unique stimulus.
entries.unit: minutes non-silence; minutes total; presentations; presentations per stimulus
entries.condition: Subject A, Gump stimulus presentations; 382 unique stimuli from the same two speakers.

entries.text: Gump data for subject B: 50 minutes non-silence, 92 minutes total, 868 presentations, mean 2.27 presentations per unique stimulus.
entries.unit: minutes non-silence; minutes total; presentations; presentations per stimulus
entries.condition: Subject B, Gump stimulus presentations; 382 unique stimuli from the same two speakers.

entries.text: Gump data for subject C: 50 minutes non-silence, 92 minutes total, 867 presentations, mean 2.27 presentations per unique stimulus.
entries.unit: minutes non-silence; minutes total; presentations; presentations per stimulus
entries.condition: Subject C, Gump stimulus presentations; 382 unique stimuli from the same two speakers.

entries.text: The target set has 39 phonemic labels: 38 Arpabet phonemes plus /sp/ for silence; phonemes are also grouped into eight descriptive phonetic categories; TIMIT silence tokens collapse to /sp/ and /zh/ maps to /sh/.
entries.condition: TIMIT and Gump; Gump transcriptions forced-aligned and manually segmented; low-frequency TIMIT /zh/ mapped to /sh/.

entries.text: The 39 phonemes are grouped into eight disjoint descriptive phonetic categories for analysis.
entries.condition: Analytical grouping of the 39 labels; categories listed in Table 2.

entries.text: TIMIT /zh/ occurred at fewer than 0.15% of time points and was absent from Gump, so all TIMIT /zh/ labels were mapped to /sh/.
entries.condition: Training/evaluation label mapping for the 39-phoneme inventory.

entries.text: Preprocessing downsampled ECoG to 400 Hz, notch-filtered 60 Hz and harmonics, visually rejected noisy channels, common-average referenced, extracted eight 70–150 Hz Gaussian-filtered analytic amplitudes, downsampled to 100 Hz, z-scored each channel per experimental session, soft-despiked, then used the first SVD component across bands.
entries.unit: Hz; Hz; filters; Hz; Hz; SD despike threshold
entries.condition: Channel z-scoring is reported per session; the paper does not state that normalization parameters were fit on training-only data.

entries.text: Speech-responsive channels were selected by a speech-versus-silence t-test on each subject's Gump responses; the magnitude threshold was 2.54, selected qualitatively after visual inspection.
entries.condition: Channel selection used Gump speech/silence labels, including the same stimulus set later used for final Gump cross-validation.

entries.text: After channel selection, subjects A, B, and C had 95, 89, and 74 relevant electrodes, respectively; over half per subject were in STG.
entries.unit: channels per subject; percent of relevant channels in STG
entries.condition: Relevant channels determined using each subject's Gump speech-versus-silence data.
entries.quote: After these steps, subjects A, B, and C had 95, 89, and 74 relevant channels, respectively.

entries.text: Ten-fold stimulus-level cross-validation used approximately 90% of stimuli for training and the remainder for testing, with each stimulus in the test fold exactly once; folds were stratified by speaker gender for TIMIT and by word/phrase/dialog class and gender for Gump.
entries.condition: Splits are described by stimulus, not by subject session or individual speaker identity.
entries.quote: Each stimulus appeared in the test data for exactly one of the folds.

entries.text: HGW grid search varied initial delay 0–490 ms, duration 0–490 ms, and window size 1–25 points; parameter steps were 10 ms, with invalid windows and points at or beyond 500 ms excluded.
entries.unit: ms delay; ms duration; points; ms increments; ms maximum offset
entries.condition: Optimal feature window selected separately per subject by average posteriogram accuracy on one arbitrarily chosen TIMIT cross-validation fold.

entries.text: Subject A's selected HGW uses 70 ms delay, 180 ms duration, four points at 70/130/190/250 ms; selected HGS offset is 100 ms.
entries.unit: ms; ms; points; ms offsets; ms HGS offset
entries.condition: Feature parameters selected for subject A using one TIMIT fold and posteriogram accuracy.

entries.text: Subject B's selected HGW uses 10 ms delay, 230 ms duration, six points at 10/60/100/150/190/240 ms; selected HGS offset is 90 ms.
entries.unit: ms; ms; points; ms offsets; ms HGS offset
entries.condition: Feature parameters selected for subject B using one TIMIT fold and posteriogram accuracy.

entries.text: Subject C's selected HGW uses 0 ms delay, 210 ms duration, five points at 0/50/100/160/210 ms; selected HGS offset is 120 ms.
entries.unit: ms; ms; points; ms offsets; ms HGS offset
entries.condition: Feature parameters selected for subject C using one TIMIT fold and posteriogram accuracy.

entries.text: The phoneme likelihood model is LDA fit to continuous feature vectors and phoneme labels, with class-specific multivariate Gaussian means and a shared covariance; class priors are relative label frequencies in training data.
entries.condition: LDA is closed form with no tunable parameters; priors may vary between cross-validation folds.

entries.text: The phonemic LM training corpus contained approximately 4.3 million sentences, 76.9 million non-silence phonemes, and 81.2 million tokens including /sp/; exact Gump stimulus sequences were excluded.
entries.value: approximately 4.3 million; about 76.9 million; about 81.2 million
entries.unit: sentences; non-silence phonemes; phoneme tokens including /sp/
entries.condition: SUBTLEX-US sentences phonetized with Festival; short/unphonetizable sentences excluded; /ax/→/ah/, /zh/→/sh/; exact Gump sequences removed.
entries.quote: Approximately 4.3 million sentences were included, resulting in a phoneme corpus with about 76.9 million non-silence phonemes (a total of about 81.2 million phoneme tokens when /sp/ is included).

entries.text: The authors chose a basic additive-smoothed 4-gram phonemic LM after comparing basic and modified Kneser–Ney orders 1–5; best reported perplexity was 20.33 on concatenated TIMIT phonemic transcriptions.
entries.unit: gram order; tested n-gram orders; perplexity
entries.condition: LM test corpus concatenated transcriptions of 499 TIMIT stimuli with silence between stimuli; lower perplexity is better.

entries.text: The deployed-in-decoder LM is the basic additive-smoothing 4-gram with δ=0.1 and interpolation weights λ4=5/9, λ3=4/7, λ2=3/5.
entries.condition: Phonemic sequence LM; /sp/ token included; no phoneme durations in LM sequences.

entries.text: Viterbi decoding initializes at /sp/, uses beam criterion 50 and retains at most 100 paths; tuned parameters are LM scale, phoneme insertion penalty, and self-transition probability.
entries.condition: Grid search evaluated TIMIT-derived likelihoods with L in {0, 0.2, 0.25, 0.333, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, P from −7 to 2, and s from 0 to 0.9 by 0.1.
entries.quote: Afterwards, we only retained a maximum of 100 of the most likely paths between iterations.

entries.text: The selected Viterbi settings were MFCC L=2/P=−1/s=0.4; subject A L=2/P=−1/s=0.3; B L=2/P=−1/s=0.9; C L=3/P=−1/s=0.1; all-subject features L=2/P=−2/s=0.4.
entries.unit: LM scaling factor; insertion penalty; self-transition probability
entries.condition: Settings selected by decoder grid search using TIMIT cross-validation likelihoods; the 'All' condition uses features from all subjects.

entries.text: PER is Levenshtein substitutions+deletions+insertions divided by reference phonemes after removing silence and consecutive repeated labels; posteriogram accuracy is frame accuracy excluding silence; confusion accuracy averages row-normalized diagonal values excluding silence. PER/posteriogram statistics use per-stimulus results, while confusion accuracy uses the overall confusion-matrix diagonal.
entries.condition: The paper also reports alternative silence-inclusive metrics in supplementary Tables S1–S2, not present in supplied text extraction; primary Table 5 values are percentages reported as mean±SD.

entries.text: The authors define chance as predicting the most frequent non-silence training phoneme, /s/, at every time point; they note uniform choice among 38 non-silence phonemes would be about 2.6% frame accuracy.
entries.unit: % accuracy under uniform selection among 38 non-silence phonemes
entries.condition: Their actual reported chance baseline is the training-set majority non-silence class /s/, not uniform random guessing.

entries.text: Final performance evaluation used all 10 Gump folds, comparing single-trial and presentation-averaged HGS/HGW features for each subject and concatenated all-subject features, plus MFCCs; both framewise estimates and Viterbi decodings were scored.
entries.condition: Two Gump speakers; 39 labels; silence excluded from the three main metrics; no random seeds reported.
entries.quote: Each evaluation used all 10 of the Gump cross-validation folds.

entries.text: A single illustrated subject-A HGW decoding of the Gump female-speaker utterance 'What is the address?' had posteriogram accuracy 48.6% and PER 50.0%.
entries.condition: One example utterance, subject A HGW, female speaker, Gump; not an aggregate result.

entries.text: Table 5 chance baseline: estimation and decoding each had PER 97.12±5.34%, posteriogram accuracy 7.06±9.77%, and confusion accuracy 2.63±16.01%.
entries.condition: Gump 10-fold evaluation; majority non-silence /s/ prediction; 39-label task, with silence excluded from scored metrics.

entries.text: Authors report HGWs significantly outperform HGSs on every subject set and metric (one-tailed Wilcoxon, p<0.005); they conclude temporal information improves neural phoneme recognition in these evaluations.
entries.condition: Gump evaluation; all subject sets including concatenated features; all three metrics; each evaluation uses 10 folds.
entries.quote: All of the HGW results were signiﬁcantly better than the HGS results for all subject sets and metrics (Wilcoxon, p < 0.005).

entries.text: HGW decoding beat HGS estimation across all subject sets (Wilcoxon, p<10−6); decoding improved PER for every subject set (p<10−11), but posteriogram accuracy did not improve consistently.
entries.condition: Gump evaluation across single-trial/averaged and individual/concatenated subject sets; PER, frame accuracy, confusion metrics reported separately.

entries.text: Decoding PER was significantly better than framewise estimation PER for all subject sets (p<10−11); confusion accuracy also improved except for averaged HGWs from C and concatenated HGWs, while many posteriogram differences were nonsignificant or negative.
entries.condition: Gump; comparison of Viterbi MAP sequences with LDA framewise argmax estimates.

entries.text: The authors interpret language modeling/Viterbi's main benefit as temporal smoothing: it generally helps PER and confusion accuracy, not framewise posteriogram accuracy; they state basic class priors were similarly effective for framewise classification.
entries.condition: Phoneme-level decoding; 4-gram LM; conclusions based on comparisons between estimates and decodings.
entries.quote: Altogether, these results indicate that temporal smoothing of the phoneme likelihoods is the primary beneﬁt of incorporating a phoneme-level LM and performing Viterbi decoding.

entries.text: Averaged neural features improved posteriogram accuracy over single-trial features for every subject (Welch p<0.01); decoding PER also improved except for subject C HGWs, while most confusion-accuracy and estimation-PER comparisons did not.
entries.condition: Gump; within-subject single-trial versus across-presentation averaged neural responses.

entries.text: Concatenating features from all three subjects significantly outperformed individual-subject features on every metric except estimation PER (p<10−5); the authors call concatenated results an upper limit, while noting pooling is infeasible for a prosthesis.
entries.condition: Gump; averaged and single-trial conditions; concatenated feature vectors include the three participants.

entries.text: MFCCs significantly outperformed neural features for each metric except estimation PER (p<10−5); neural features exceeded the majority-class chance baseline in most but not all comparisons.
entries.condition: Gump; acoustic MFCC comparator versus neural HGS/HGW features; stated exceptions include all estimation-PER comparisons, some single-trial confusion scores, and subject-B single-trial HGS estimation accuracy.

entries.text: For averaged HGWs from subject B, phoneme time position had a negative relation to frame accuracy (β=−0.792, p<10−10); across all neural feature evaluations β<−0.4 and p<10−5. MFCCs showed β=0.051, p=0.225.
entries.condition: Estimated posteriograms on 382 Gump stimuli; utterance onset defined after ≥500 ms silence; non-silence time points; mixed-effects logistic regression with stimulus random intercepts and slopes.

entries.text: Speaker-gender analyses found strong gender effects for MFCCs, but most neural-feature comparisons showed no significant difference; the authors infer that speaker identity does not significantly affect their neural-feature system, while acknowledging the test used only two Gump speakers.
entries.condition: Three within-speaker 10-fold evaluations and two cross-gender train/test evaluations; two speakers total, one male and one female.

entries.text: The authors limit confidence in the selected HGW conclusion because of constrained window parameterization, LDA's linearity assumption, and the relatively small TIMIT grid-search data; shared window parameters across electrodes may miss heterogeneous STG responses.
entries.condition: Feature-window search and LDA evaluation; discussed as limits on inference about optimal temporal representations.

entries.text: The authors state that averaging trials and pooling subjects are relatively infeasible for prosthetic use; results from concatenated subjects represent an upper limit under current physical/methodological constraints.
entries.condition: Deployment discussion; present evaluation uses offline data from three subjects and averaged or concatenated features.
entries.quote: However, averaging and combining features across multiple subjects are relatively infeasible approaches for a speech prosthetic application.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that neural-frame accuracy degrades as an utterance progresses and identify this as particularly problematic for continuous speech decoding; its cause is unresolved.
entries.condition: Observed for neural but not MFCC features; proposed explanations include transient onset responses, overlapping phoneme responses, lexical information, and phonotactics.

entries.text: Authors concede that the system's performance is limited and that feature representations/models remain simple; they propose word-level LM, more advanced ASR models, covert speech, and single-subject single-trial methods as future work.
entries.condition: Current work uses phoneme-level output and perceived speech, not covert speech or word-level decoding.

entries.text: No random seeds, repeated independent split runs, or run-to-run variability protocol is reported; the paper describes one 10-fold cross-validation construction per dataset/analysis.
entries.condition: Applies to TIMIT parameter selection and Gump final evaluation; folds are stimulus-level.

entries.text: The paper does not report speaker-disjoint TIMIT folds or identify speaker identities per fold; Gump's ordinary folds split stimuli from the same two speakers across train/test. Cross-gender tests are reported separately.
entries.condition: TIMIT folds balance male/female sample types; Gump folds balance type and gender, not speaker identity.

entries.text: The channel-selection t-test uses the entire Gump set, while final evaluation also cross-validates Gump; the paper does not give a training-fold-only channel-selection procedure or quantify this selection/evaluation overlap.
entries.condition: Potential selection leakage: relevant electrodes are selected from all Gump speech/silence samples before reported Gump 10-fold evaluation.
entries.quote: we divided each subject’s high gamma activity during perception of the Gump set into speech and silence subsets using the phonemic transcriptions of the stimuli.

entries.text: HGW settings were chosen by test-fold posteriogram accuracy on one arbitrarily selected TIMIT fold, and Viterbi settings were optimized on TIMIT cross-validation results; no independent validation set is described.
entries.condition: The TIMIT fold used for feature selection is part of the stated cross-validation scheme; validation/test role separation is not described.
entries.quote: using the neural responses recorded from that subject during each stimulus presentation speciﬁed by one arbitrarily-chosen TIMIT cross-validation fold.

entries.text: Neural channels are z-scored per experimental session, but the paper does not state whether means/standard deviations are estimated on training data only or whether held-out test samples contribute; MFCC normalization is also unspecified.
entries.condition: Session-wise z-scoring reported in preprocessing; train/test fold construction is stimulus-level.
entries.quote: individually z-scored each channel across each experimental session.

entries.text: The paper refers to experimental sessions and performs session-wise normalization but does not report the number of sessions per subject, session boundaries, or whether sessions are held out between train and test.
entries.condition: Cross-validation is specified by stimulus rather than by recording session.
entries.quote: individually z-scored each channel across each experimental session.

entries.text: The paper specifies chance baselines, metric definitions, alpha=0.01, and one-tailed tests, but does not report a correction for the many cross-condition significance tests except Bonferroni correction in speaker-gender post-hoc tests.
entries.condition: Multiple paired/unpaired comparisons across metrics, subjects, and feature conditions.

entries.text: No user confirmation mechanism is described; the system outputs an automatically decoded phoneme sequence without a confirmation stage.
entries.condition: Offline research pipeline; no user-facing interactive deployment evaluation.

entries.text: No user correction or online adaptation process is described; the model is evaluated through offline cross-validation only.
entries.condition: No interactive correction data or deployment trial is reported.

entries.text: The system's output is a discrete phoneme sequence (MAP estimate); it does not directly output words or reconstructed acoustics.
entries.condition: Phoneme-level continuous decoding of perceived speech; no word-level language model or speech synthesis is implemented.

entries.text: Raw cortical recordings were acquired at approximately 3052 Hz before downsampling.
entries.condition: ECoG local field potentials during speech perception tasks.

entries.text: The acoustic comparator uses 39-dimensional MFCC vectors including energy, velocity, and acceleration features.
entries.condition: MFCC comparator for the same Gump test stimuli; neural features are ECoG-derived.

questions.q: Does the paper's evidence support a general claim that temporal windows improve neural phoneme decoding?
questions.answer: Within the reported Gump evaluation, yes: HGWs significantly beat HGSs across all subjects and metrics (p<0.005). The authors limit confidence because HGW selection used a small TIMIT fold and shared parameterization, and channel selection used the Gump set later evaluated.

questions.q: How much does the language model improve the system, and on which outcome?
questions.answer: Viterbi/LM decoding improves sequence PER across subject sets and often confusion accuracy, but does not consistently improve framewise posteriogram accuracy. The authors interpret the main benefit as temporal smoothing. MFCCs remain stronger than neural features on most reported outcomes.

questions.q: What is the strongest reported neural result, and what does it measure?
questions.answer: Concatenated averaged HGWs yielded decoding posteriogram accuracy 29.26±14.88% and confusion accuracy 25.03±10.69%, with PER 70.47±16.77%, on Gump 10-fold evaluation. This is a multi-subject offline upper bound, not a single-subject prosthetic result.

questions.q: Are the reported test results speaker-independent and free of selection overlap?
questions.answer: Not established. Ordinary folds split stimuli, and Gump uses the same two speakers across train/test; speaker-disjoint TIMIT folds are not reported. Relevant electrodes are selected using all Gump data before Gump evaluation, and the paper does not describe fold-specific selection.

questions.q: Which evaluation reproducibility details are missing?
questions.answer: Random seeds/repeated split runs, session counts and session-held-out testing, train-only normalization details, and an independent validation set are not reported. The paper does state its chance baseline and its primary metric definitions.

questions.q: Writer lookup: does any decoding result at LM scale L=0 appear in the paper?
questions.answer: No; the grid includes L=0 (Sec. 2.2.3) but Table 5 reports only the selected settings (Table 4).

questions.q: Writer lookup: which earlier NSR works do the authors credit, and how?
questions.answer: Herff et al. 2015 [9] (production, restricted vocabulary) and Chang et al. 2015 [10] (perception, multi-speaker, ICSI technical report, not in the wiki).
